w: Dr. Abou-Arraj taught this in two parts. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): gum thickness, receding gums and how they're grafted, missing firm gum, and the frenum. The last two problems, too much gum and gum discoloration, he covers in a live class the week of Nov 9. Until that class is posted, those parts come from his slides and the class exam-review guide. The tissues The mucogingival junction (MGJ) is the line between the firm, pink gum (gingiva) and the loose, redder lining of the mouth (alveolar mucosa). You can often see it, but a probe finds it best. All the gum above that line is keratinized gingiva, the tough kind. Part of it is stuck down to the tooth and bone (attached gingiva); the edge is free (free gingiva), and that's where the probe slips in to measure pocket depth. Gum and lining problems Periodontal plastic therapy fixes mucogingival deformities: anything abnormal about the amount, size, outline or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The current classification (the 2017 World Workshop) lists seven: (1) gum thickness and shape (the phenotype); (2) receding gums (recession); (3) not enough firm gum (lack of keratinized gingiva); (4) a shallow vestibule; (5) a frenum or muscle attached too high; (6) too much gum (gingival excess); and (7) discolored gum (a tattoo). Thin or thick gums The phenotype is how thick the gum is (thin or thick) and how its edge is shaped (scalloped or flat). To test thickness, put the probe in the pocket. If you can see the probe through the gum, it's thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't, it's thick, more than 1 mm. It matters because thin gum recedes more easily, and recession on thin gum tends to get worse; thick gum resists it. His example: a young patient with gum so thin you could see the roots was about to get braces. Braces plus years of brushing could make his gums recede, so before the braces the gum was made thicker: a flap was lifted, a piece of connective tissue from the palate was stitched over the two front teeth most at risk, and the flap was laid back over it. Two weeks later the gum was already thicker, and he went ahead with braces. Receding gums: what and who Recession means the gum edge has moved below the CEJ (where the enamel ends), so some root shows. Measure it from the gum edge to the CEJ at the same six spots as pocket depth. Check between the teeth too, because recession there changes what treatment can do. It's very common. The slide: 88% of people 65 and over and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one spot. In the recording: over half of Americans 30 and older have at least 1 mm, and almost a quarter have at least one spot of 3 mm or more. Older people have more because they've piled up more risk factors over the years, not because of age itself. It's more common in men and in African-Americans, and most common on the cheek side of upper molars (especially first molars) and lower front teeth; canines are common too. What sets it up The slide's list of ten: gum disease (periodontitis); injury (brushing, flossing, picking, objects); bone variations (a window or a gap in the bone over the root) and teeth out of line; not enough firm gum; thin gum; braces; past gum surgery; a frenum or muscle attached high; filling and crown edges; and chewing tobacco. What he added: Gum disease means periodontitis, not gingivitis: losing bone and attachment uncovers the root. Past gum surgery: resective surgery causes most of its recession on purpose, to leave no pockets, so the patient can keep the area clean. Brushing is the most common injury: hard bristles, or simply brushing too hard. Flossing habits, picking, objects like a fingernail or pen, and harsh medicines put right on the gum count too. Bone variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing bone from the top edge down. A tooth that sits out toward the cheek has thinner gum and gets hit harder by the brush. Moving it back into line with braces can undo some recession without a graft. Thin gum plus missing bone plus hard brushing is "the perfect storm." Braces that push teeth out of their bone over thin gum can cause recession, though some studies disagree; he calls it controversial. Crown and filling edges placed under the gum, poorly fitting, or too bulky on thin gum can cause it (not that every crown needs a graft). A high frenum tugs on the gum edge with every movement. Chewing tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower back teeth, can cause severe recession right there; his worst case had recession down to the bottom of the vestibule, with no pockets. How it happens Two ways. Brushing injury, especially on thin gum: the surface is scraped, the tissue underneath gets inflamed, a small sore forms, and with more injury the gum edge pulls back. Plaque: the same process as periodontitis, plaque left in the pocket causing attachment loss, just in one small spot on thin gum. Either way, his key word is inflammation: it's what actually causes recession. Everything on the list just sets it up. The Cairo grades: how much root can be covered? Before suggesting a graft, grade the recession, because the grade predicts the result. The Cairo system has three: RT1: no attachment lost between the teeth; you can't find the CEJ between the teeth. The best case: about 100% of the root can be covered. RT2: some attachment lost between the teeth, but no more than on the front of the tooth (the attachment loss between the teeth is less than or equal to the loss on the cheek side). You can see the CEJ between the teeth. Expect partial coverage, about 50 to 60% in his examples: only up to the level of the attachment between the teeth, because there's nothing there to hold the gum higher and no blood supply for it. RT3: more attachment lost between the teeth than on the front. A graft won't cover the root at all, so don't try for coverage. Why treat it Exposed roots and lost tissue make these more likely: (1) sensitive teeth, (2) sore gums (thin gum can hurt to brush), (3) root cavities, (4) looks, (5) harder cleaning, and (6) the gum inflames more easily. And it keeps going: a 2016 review (Chambrone and Tatakis) found untreated recession keeps getting worse. So "it doesn't hurt, let's just watch it" doesn't mean it will stay the same. Except for RT3, consider treating it when there's a reason to. (Fixing recession with fillings is next year's course.) Gum grafts: where they come from Two main sources: the patient's own tissue (an autograft) and donor tissue from a tissue bank (an allograft). Animal sources exist too. The most common graft comes from the palate, because palate tissue is the tough, keratinized kind, and its connective tissue teaches the new site to grow tough gum. Two kinds come from the palate: a free gingival graft (FGG), the surface layer plus the connective tissue in one piece; and a connective tissue graft (CTG), only the connective tissue, no surface layer. The palate's layers, from the surface down: a thin surface layer (0.3-0.6 mm), the thick connective tissue (1.25-3 mm), then fat and glands, then bone. A thick graft brings fat along, and that's trimmed off so it doesn't slow healing. Stay away from the big artery and nerve of the palate (the greater palatine). On the slide it sits about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average one and 17 mm in a high one. So a high, deep palate gives the most room for error. A CTG can be taken two ways: open a trap door and take the connective tissue from underneath, or cut out the whole piece with its surface layer and peel the surface layer off after. The exam-review guide's version: sometimes an FGG is cut but used as a CTG, because that's easier. The rule: if a flap will cover the graft, use connective tissue only, because surface layer pressed against the flap's underside won't heal. If the graft will be left uncovered, use an FGG. Covering a root: CTG under a flap pulled up His case: recession on #10 and #11. He lifted a flap, took a CTG from the palate, stitched it over the roots, and pulled the flap up over it (a coronally advanced flap), with no tension so it stays put. Four weeks later the roots were well covered, and the gum over them was much thicker, which resists more recession. His rule: "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft." Many teeth: donor skin Grafting many teeth from the palate means a big, painful harvest. Instead, use an allograft: donated human skin (dermis), cleaned of its surface layer, hair follicles and cells, leaving a framework of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers. This is acellular dermal matrix (ADM), the most common donor graft (AlloDerm is one). It was made for burns and reconstructions (since 1995) and used in dentistry since 1997. Pros: no second wound on the palate, patients accept it more, shorter surgery, many teeth at once, good-looking results, easy to use. Cons: it's "more or less a dead piece of skin," like a band-aid, with nothing alive to help healing. So it must be completely covered by the flap; over time the body replaces it with its own tissue. In a tough site it can't match the patient's own tissue (the guide: it doesn't work as well as an autograft, but has many advantages). His case: five or six teeth, canine to canine, with RT2 and RT3 recession. He used a tunnel flap: like an envelope, but without lifting the gum between the teeth, joining the pockets of all the teeth into one tunnel under the gum. The ADM was soaked in two baths (the second with the antibiotic tetracycline), slid into the tunnel, held with sling stitches, and covered by pulling the flap up. Six months later it was a good result for that starting point. Not enough firm gum Keratinized gingiva (KG) is measured from the gum edge to the MGJ. To find the MGJ, look for the color change, or roll the probe up from the loose lining: the lining rolls with it, and where it stops rolling is the MGJ. On average the upper front teeth have the most, the canine and first premolar the least, and the molars more again; the lower arch is similar, and on the tongue side of the lower jaw the front teeth have the least. Do you need it? With good plaque control and no other injury, a band of attached gum isn't essential for healthy gums. But if plaque control isn't great, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't clean perfectly, so a tooth with under 2 mm is likely to recede. Still, it's case by case: not every such tooth needs a graft. Growing firm gum: an FGG left uncovered His patient had RT2 recession, a sensitive tooth and no firm gum, so the spot trapped plaque and kept receding. The goal was a band of firm gum, with any root coverage a bonus. A CTG under a flap wouldn't help: the only tissue to cover it with was loose lining, and lining doesn't turn into firm gum by covering a graft. So he did an FGG: the flap was moved down (an apically positioned flap), and a graft with its surface layer was stitched on and left uncovered, so it heals into firm gum. The palate wound heals on its own (secondary intention). The graft is held only by stitches, so the patient shouldn't pull the lip to look at it, should eat soft food and shouldn't brush there while it heals. Three months later: a good band of firm gum, some root coverage (as expected for RT2), no more sensitivity, and a spot that's easier to clean. The frenum A frenum attached too high pulls on the gum edge every time the lip and face move, which traps plaque and makes recession worse. In one patient it was in the way of her new crowns looking good, so it was removed before the final crowns (a frenectomy): cut out the frenum in a diamond shape and close it with a few stitches into the lip. Too much gum (slides; the live class) Four causes, each with its fix. 1. Pseudopocket: swollen gums from gingivitis make the pocket deeper without any attachment loss. Fix: better home care and a cleaning. 2. Overgrowth from a drug: phenytoin (a seizure drug), calcium channel blockers (blood pressure drugs) and cyclosporine. Fix: cut away the extra gum (gingivectomy), better home care, and maybe change the drug. 3. Uneven gum lines between matching teeth. Fix: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap. 4. A gummy smile. Fix: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, once you know the cause. Gummy smile: find the cause Each cause has a sign on the slides: short teeth (altered passive eruption), with odd tooth sizes and proportions and uneven gum lines; an upper jaw grown too far down (vertical maxillary excess), with a long lower third of the face; a short upper lip, under 20 mm; a lip that lifts too far, more than 8 mm; or a mix. Gum that never moved down Normally, after a tooth comes in, the gum slowly moves down to uncover the crown and settles near the CEJ (passive eruption). In altered passive eruption it doesn't, so teeth look short. It's graded two ways. Type 1: a wide band of gum, with the MGJ below the bone edge. Type 2: a normal band, with the MGJ at the CEJ. A: the bone is more than 1 mm below the CEJ. B: the bone is right up near the CEJ. Types 1A and 1B are the most common. The fix is crown lengthening: 1A, cut away gum (gingivectomy); 2A, move the gum down with a flap (apically positioned flap); 1B and 2B, the flap plus bone reshaping. Why: in a B type the bone is too close, so it has to be moved; in Type 2 the gum band is only normal width, so cutting it away would leave too little firm gum, and the flap moves it down instead. Only 1A has extra gum and room above the bone. Before crown lengthening The clinical crown is what shows above the gum; the anatomical crown is all the enamel, down to the CEJ. Check the pocket depths, gum health and width of firm gum, and on the radiograph how deep any fracture or decay goes, the root's length and shape, where the bone is, and whether the nerve is involved. Checking the smile His checklist: face symmetry (the face in thirds; the face's midline against the teeth's midline; a long lower third means the upper jaw grew too far down); smile line (high, medium or low); edges of the front teeth (they should follow the lower lip); upper lip (20-22 mm in women, 22-24 mm in men, and it normally lifts 6-8 mm in a full smile); gum line (the central incisors and canines level, the lateral incisors 1 mm lower, toward the biting edge); and tooth shape and proportions: the golden proportion, so from the front the central, lateral and the visible part of the canine show at about 1.618 : 1 : 0.618 (the guide rounds it to 1.6, 1 and 0.6). Treating a gummy smile By cause: short teeth (altered passive eruption): crown lengthening and restorations; upper jaw too long: braces and jaw surgery, maybe with gum surgery too; lip that lifts too far: lip repositioning surgery or Botox; short upper lip: no good options. If there are several causes, combine treatments. Patient 1 A healthy 28-year-old woman who didn't like the color of her front teeth (fluorosis), didn't want braces and wanted veneers. Her face thirds were equal and her lip was normal in length and movement, but she had a high smile line, an uneven, tilted gum line and short, square front teeth. So her gummy smile came from the teeth and gums, not the jaw or lip, and the plan was crown lengthening, then veneers. The photos follow her healing out to 18 months. Discolored gum The last problem on the list: a gray stain in the gum, a tattoo. The slides show one case where the stained tissue was cut out, replaced with a graft from the palate and reshaped 3 months later.
